images.title: Two equilateral triangles make a rhombus
images.purpose: Shows two equilateral triangles of side 4 cm joined into a rhombus whose diagonals cross at right angles, with angles 60° and 120°.
images.composition: Plain white background, the main object large and centred with wide empty margins, no scenery, no characters, no extra decoration. One large rhombus in the centre lying on its side, with both diagonals drawn as in the diagonal lab.
images.exact_structure: One rhombus in dark outline lying flat, about 1.73 times as wide as it is tall, with sharp corners at left and right and blunt corners at top and bottom. Each side carries one identical short tick mark; the label 4 cm sits beside the top left side. The short vertical diagonal is a thick teal (#0072B2) line labelled 4 cm, splitting the rhombus into two equilateral triangles: the left triangle is lightly filled teal and the right triangle lightly filled amber (#E69F00). The long horizontal diagonal is a plain thin dark line. The diagonals cross at O, marked with a small filled reddish purple (#CC79A7) square right angle mark. A small arc labelled 60° at the left corner and a larger arc labelled 120° at the top corner, both in reddish purple. No corner letters. Nothing else in the frame.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: Two equilateral triangles of 4 cm give a rhombus with all sides 4 cm and angles 60° and 120°.
images.description: Shows two equilateral triangles of side 4 cm joined into a rhombus whose diagonals cross at right angles, with angles 60° and 120°.
images.context: Angles 60°, 60° + 60° = 120°, 60°, 120°; diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at 90°.

image_decisions.why: The diagonal lab's crossing diagonals plus the practice's two equilateral triangles in one clean figure.
